plan.interpretation: A frontend developer comes away able to make their own UIs look noticeably more polished by applying core visual design principles (hierarchy, spacing, typography, color) and by critiquing and redesigning real interfaces.
assumptions: 'Design' means UI/visual design for web apps, not graphic design, UX research, or brand design
The learner wants to improve the look of interfaces they build in code, so developer-oriented design content fits best
Because they know CSS, layout mechanics are skipped and the focus is on design decisions
'Nothing older than 2020' means videos published in 2020 or later
No design tool such as Figma is assumed; tool basics are included only as far as needed to follow redesigns

sub_topics.title: Visual hierarchy and layout composition
sub_topics.why: They can build any layout with Flexbox and Grid, but need to learn how to guide the eye with size, weight, contrast and emphasis.

sub_topics.title: Spacing, alignment and consistent spacing scales
sub_topics.why: Inconsistent spacing is the most common reason developer-built UIs look amateur, and a spacing scale maps directly onto CSS variables.

sub_topics.title: Typography for interfaces
sub_topics.why: Font choice, type scale, line height and line length strongly affect polish and readability and are easy to apply in CSS.

sub_topics.title: Color systems, contrast and accessibility
sub_topics.why: They need a practical way to build palettes, shades and accessible contrast rather than picking colors by guesswork.

sub_topics.title: Polish details: shadows, borders, radius, and icons
sub_topics.why: Small refinements make UIs feel finished, and they translate directly into CSS properties.

sub_topics.title: Critiquing existing UIs and spotting problems
sub_topics.why: Learning to diagnose what is wrong with a real interface builds the design eye and satisfies the need for practical critique.

sub_topics.title: Full redesign of a real UI, step by step
sub_topics.why: Watching principles applied end to end on a real interface shows how to combine them and gives a repeatable process.

[00:33] (chapter) What is UI UX?
[00:42] (chapter) What is UI?
[01:01] (chapter) What is UX?
[01:40] (chapter) Sam's problem with the website designed by students
[02:02] (chapter) Sam's realization about UI UX to fix the the problem
[02:19] (chapter) Understanding the Users
[03:12] (chapter) Sketching the Plan / Wireframing
[04:07] (chapter) Choosing Right Look / Visual Design
[04:58] (chapter) Organizing Screens / Information Architecture
[05:45] (chapter) Testing and Improving (Usability Testing)
[00:00] Hi there. Meet Sam. Sam is a curious college student who loves technology, but doesn't really know much about how things are designed on apps and websites. One day, Sam's best friend showed them a clunky old website. It was hard to read. Buttons didn't work properly, and the colors hurt Sam's eyes. Sam said, "Why is this website so
[00:23] bad?" Sam started doing research online trying to understand how websites are designed and how they can improve. That's when Sam stumbled into the exciting world of UI and UX. Let's go on a journey with Sam to find out what UIUX is and why it's so important. Sam learned that UI
[00:44] stands for user interface. It's what you see on a screen, buttons, colors, text, and layout. Think of it like the controls on a video game or the dashboard of a car. If the interface is welldesigned, you know exactly where to press or click without even thinking about it. UX, on the other hand, stands
[01:04] for user experience. It's all about how you feel when using a website or an app. Does it make your life easier or harder? For example, if you can easily find what you're looking for, the UX is good. If you feel confused or frustrated, the UX isn't doing its job. Together, UI and UX
[01:27] are like the perfect recipe. UI is the presentation, the look and feel, while UX is the flavor, making sure the whole experience is enjoyable and effective. Sam had an idea for an app that helps students organize their homework. But every time they showed the app design to their friends, the feedback was
[01:48] disappointing. The buttons were too small to tap. Nobody could figure out where to add assignments. The colors were so bright that it hurt their eyes. The app felt messy, like too much was happening on one screen. Sam realized something important. The way the app looked, UI, and the way it worked, UX,
[02:12] weren't right. That's when Sam decided to dive into the world of UIUX to fix it. Sam realized that to create a great homework organization app, they needed to start by understanding what users truly wanted. Instead of guessing, Sam decided to talk to their friends, asking them questions like, "How do you
[02:33] currently organize your homework?" "What frustrates you about it?" They also observed their friends using similar apps to see what worked well and what didn't. To make this process easier, Sam used tools like Google Forms to create surveys and collect feedback and notion to organize the responses into
[02:54] categories like must-have features and common issues. By the end of this research, Sam discovered that users wanted an app that was simple, fast, and visually calming with features like an easy way to add assignments and a color coding system for subjects. With a clear understanding of user needs, Sam moved
[03:15] on to sketching a plan for the app. This stage, called wireframing, was all about creating a basic outline of the app's structure without worrying about colors or details. Sam drew a rough sketch of the home screen, ensuring it had large, clear buttons for essential actions like add assignment and view calendar. They also
[03:39] planned a smooth navigation flow so users could easily move from one screen to another without feeling lost. To bring these sketches to life, Sam used tools like Figma, a beginner-friendly tool for creating digital wireframes, and Balsami, which allowed them to brainstorm quickly with handdrawn style
[04:00] designs. This step helped Sam focus on the app's structure and how users would interact with it. Once the wireframes were ready, it was time to think about how the app would look. This stage, called visual design, was about choosing colors, fonts, and icons that would make the app visually appealing and
[04:22] userfriendly. Sam selected soft pastel colors to create a calming vibe and picked clean, simple fonts that were easy to read, even on small screens. To make the app more intuitive, they added friendly, recognizable icons such as a calendar icon for the view calendar
[04:42] button. Sam relied on tools like Canva to experiment with different visual styles and create mood boards and coolers to generate harmonious color schemes. This step ensured the app looked professional and consistent while being pleasant to use. While the app's design was taking shape, Sam noticed
[05:03] that users had trouble finding what they needed in the earlier version. To fix this, they focused on information architecture, which involves organizing the app's screens logically. Sam mapped out the flow of the app so that the home screen offered two clear options, add assignment and view
[05:23] calendar, while less frequently used actions like settings were tucked into a drop- down menu. To visualize this flow, Sam used Miro, a digital whiteboard tool that helped them create a clear and logical layout. This organization made it easier for users to find what they were looking for without feeling
[05:45] overwhelmed. Finally, with a fully designed app, Sam needed to make sure it worked well in realworld use. This step, called usability testing, involved giving the app prototype to their friends and observing how they interacted with it. Sam gathered valuable feedback such as suggestions to
[06:06] make the save button bigger and requests for a color coding feature to organize assignments by subject. To facilitate this testing, Sam used tools like Maze, which provided detailed reports on how users navigated the app, and Zoom to record their friends interactions. Based on this feedback, Sam made the
[06:28] necessary changes and tested the app again. After several iterations, users found the app simple, intuitive, and effective. After following these steps and using these tools, Sam's app transformed. What was once a confusing and cluttered design became a
[06:48] userfriendly, visually appealing, and highly functional app. Sam's friends now found it super easy to organize their homework. They loved the intuitive flow, the calming colors, and the big clear buttons. By understanding user needs, creating wireframes, designing
[07:10] thoughtfully, and testing the app, Sam turned their idea into something truly useful. This is the power of UIUX. It helps solve real problems and creates designs that people love to use. Which tool is best for creating wireframes and app designs? A. Google Forms, B. Figma,
[07:31] C. Canva, D Maze. Let us know your answer in the comments below, and three lucky winners will get a chance to win an Amazon voucher. We hope that you enjoyed this video and found it informative and exciting. If yes, then we would appreciate a thumbs up, a gentle
[07:53] reminder to get subscribed to SimplyLearn and click that bell icon to never miss any updates from SimplyLearn.

Understanding visual hierarchy is crucial when learning graphic design, layout design, UI design, motion design, or any other visual communication medium. In visual communication, we don’t get a lot of time to convey a message. In addition, our vocabulary of design elements is highly subjective and open to viewer interpretation. So visual hierarchy is a great tool to help you communicate clearly. It governs how the elements of a composition are organized to guide the viewer's eye and ensure they receive the message the designer intended.

pool.description:
In this video, I break down 8 color theory laws every UI/UX design, UX design, and graphic design beginner needs to know, and every working designer should revisit.

Color isn't decoration, it's the first thing your brain judges before it even reads a headline, and most people are doing it completely wrong.

I used to pick colors by vibe too, until I learned there's real psychology behind why some palettes feel intentional and others feel like a scam. 

We'll get into the science of first impressions, why certain color combos quietly fight your users, how dark mode breaks all your old rules, and the one mistake almost every AI-generated interface makes right now, so keep watching till the end!

02:36 Color Theory Basics
11:04 Rule 2
12:27 Rule 3

16:44 Rule 5
18:26 Rule 6
20:18 Rule 7
22:27 Rule 8
24:54 Conclusion
25:51 Outro

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simultaneous_contrast

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmholtz%E2%80%93Kohlrausch_effect

https://www.interaction-design.org/literature/topics/gestalt-principles

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_wheel

pool.title: Beginning Graphic Design: Layout & Composition
pool.description:
A good design is about more than choosing the right colours, fonts, or images. The way you arrange everything on a page can make the difference between a design that feels cluttered and one that is clear, balanced, and easy to follow.🎨

In this video, we explore the basics of layout and composition in graphic design. You'll discover how spacing, alignment, contrast, and repetition work together to create designs that look professional and help people find the information they need.

In this video, you'll discover:
How proximity helps group related information
Why white space makes designs easier to read
How alignment and grids keep your layouts organized
How contrast draws attention to important details
How visual hierarchy guides the viewer's eye
How repetition creates a consistent look across your designs

These principles are useful whether you're creating presentations, posters, social media graphics, documents, or website layouts. You don't need to be a professional designer to start using them.🎨

pool.title: Super Practical Guide to Color Theory, Color Models and Perfect Color Palettes | UI Design
pool.description:
Maybe you’ve followed all the color harmony and color theory tutorials to a tee and generated a complementary color palette, but you notice that the colors don’t seem to match very well, perhaps they look harsh or a bit muddy and unprofessional and you don’t really know why.  

The part that's often missing is understanding tone, tint, shade and temperature 

What I discovered is that on digital screens, there is a formula and safe range of Saturation and Brightness that will result in a perfect palette for each category every time.

In this super practical guide, I'll show you how to setup your design apps (Sketch or Figma) and create color palettes that match every single time. Using a few tricks and a few numbers.

pool.title: Steal My UI/UX Process in 2026 (Real Project Breakdown)
pool.description:
I’m breaking down my real UI/UX process in 2026, end to end.

Tools used:
Mobbin http://mobbin.com/agatha ( aff )
Figma 

This is a project I’m actively working on — a healthcare product that needs to work across mobile and dashboard, with strict accessibility, branding constraints, and very specific users. No fake case study, no theory.


0:00 This took me 12 years to learn
0:36 The real project & constraints
1:00 How I research UX properly
2:55 Why I skip wireframes
3:45 Feedback that changed everything
4:44 When branding breaks UX
5:53 Motion & polish
7:01 Before vs after
7:17 How I hand off to devs
8:06 Shipping & final thoughts

You’ll see:

How I start every project by reading the PRD and understanding constraints
Why I always analyse full app flows, not single screens
How I use Mobbin to research real apps and UX patterns
Why I skip low-fi wireframes and go straight into high-fi
How feedback completely changed some key screens
How I work with branding limitations (fonts, colors, accessibility)
How I add motion, onboarding animations, and polish

How I prepare everything for developers so they can actually build it

By the end, you’ll see the before vs after — from a rough prototype to a fully designed, production-ready app.

If you’re a UI/UX designer, product designer, founder, or PM, feel free to steal the process — just not the app idea 🙂

Let me know in the comments if you want a deeper breakdown of any specific step.

🔗 Want my full process for finding clients and delivering elite websites? Sign up for the waitlist:  https://selfmadewebdesigner.com/waitlist
